title: Nervous System
tagline: Sensory and motor systems, stroke, epilepsy, headache, movement disorders, neuroinflammation, dementia and neuromuscular disease
summary: Neurological disease affects how people move, feel, think and communicate. This course links the organisation of the sensory and motor systems to the neurological examination, and then to the common disorders of the nervous system: stroke, epilepsy, headache, movement disorders, multiple sclerosis and infection, dementia and motor neuron disease, and diseases of nerve and muscle.
overview: Neurology localises before it diagnoses. The anatomy of the nervous system is a map: each symptom and sign places the problem somewhere on it, and knowing where the lesion is narrows down what it could be. The first two lessons teach that method, through the sensory pathways, vision and hearing, the motor pathways, the cranial nerves and the neurological examination.

The remaining lessons apply it to the conditions that fill neurology clinics and wards. Stroke covers recognition, thrombolysis and thrombectomy, intracerebral and subarachnoid haemorrhage and secondary prevention. Epilepsy covers seizure classification, first seizures, antiseizure medicines and status epilepticus. Headache and pain covers migraine, cluster headache, dangerous secondary headaches and medication overuse. Movement disorders covers Parkinson's disease, tremor, dystonia and chorea. Neuroinflammation covers multiple sclerosis, neuromyelitis optica, autoimmune encephalitis, meningitis and encephalitis. Dementia and neurodegeneration covers the dementias, motor neuron disease, the ataxias and prion disease, and the final lesson covers peripheral nerve, neuromuscular junction and muscle disease.

Each lesson works through clinical cases with step-by-step solutions, follows current UK guidance (mainly NICE), and ends with exercises that practise localisation, interpretation of tests such as CSF, nerve conduction studies and imaging, and the principles of treatment.
outcomes: Describe the sensory and motor pathways and use them to localise a lesion from the history and examination: cortex, internal capsule, brainstem, spinal cord, root, plexus, nerve, neuromuscular junction or muscle.
Examine the cranial nerves and interpret common abnormalities, including visual field defects, pupil abnormalities, double vision, facial weakness, hearing loss and vertigo.

Recognise acute stroke and TIA, explain the time-dependent benefits and risks of thrombolysis and thrombectomy, distinguish ischaemic stroke from intracerebral and subarachnoid haemorrhage, and outline secondary prevention.

Classify seizures and epilepsies, assess a first seizure, explain the main antiseizure medicines and their safety issues, including valproate in pregnancy, and manage status epilepticus by a staged protocol.
Diagnose migraine, tension-type and cluster headache, apply red flags for secondary headache, and describe acute and preventive treatment, including medication overuse headache.
Explain basal ganglia circuitry, diagnose and manage Parkinson's disease and its motor complications, and recognise atypical parkinsonism, essential tremor, dystonia and Huntington's disease.

Apply dissemination in space and time to multiple sclerosis, recognise optic neuritis, NMOSD and autoimmune encephalitis, interpret CSF findings, and give immediate treatment for bacterial meningitis and viral encephalitis.

Assess cognitive impairment, distinguish the common dementias, outline motor neuron disease, ataxia and prion disease, and diagnose and manage neuropathies, Guillain-Barre syndrome, myasthenia gravis and myopathies.

history.title: An essay on the shaking palsy
history.detail: The London physician James Parkinson described six people with rest tremor, flexed posture and a hurrying gait, which he called paralysis agitans. Friedrich Lewy described the inclusions now named after him in 1912, and the loss of brain dopamine was shown in 1960.

history.title: Speech and the left frontal lobe
history.detail: Paul Broca examined the brain of a patient who for many years could say only the syllable 'tan', and found a lesion in the left inferior frontal gyrus. It was the first widely accepted localisation of a function to a region of cortex.

history.title: Electrical stimulation of the motor cortex
history.detail: Gustav Fritsch and Eduard Hitzig showed that electrical stimulation of a dog's cortex caused movements of the opposite side of the body. With John Hughlings Jackson's study of seizures that march from one body part to the next, this established that the motor cortex is organised as a map.

history.title: The neuron doctrine
history.detail: Wilhelm Waldeyer coined the term neuron and, drawing on Santiago Ramon y Cajal's studies with Camillo Golgi's silver stain, argued that the nervous system is made of separate cells that communicate across gaps rather than a continuous network.

history.title: The human electroencephalogram
history.detail: Hans Berger, a psychiatrist in Jena, first recorded the electrical activity of the human brain through the scalp in 1924 and published his findings, including the alpha rhythm, in 1929. EEG became a basic tool in epilepsy and intensive care.

history.title: The cortical homunculus
history.detail: Wilder Penfield and Edwin Boldrey published maps of the sensory and motor cortex made by stimulating the brains of awake patients during epilepsy surgery in Montreal, showing an orderly but distorted representation of the body.

history.title: The ionic basis of the nerve impulse
history.detail: Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley used the squid giant axon and the voltage clamp to show how sodium and potassium currents generate the action potential. Their work explains how many anaesthetics and antiseizure medicines act.

history.title: Levodopa for Parkinson's disease
history.detail: After Ole Hornykiewicz and colleagues showed dopamine deficiency in the striatum of people with Parkinson's disease, George Cotzias showed that gradually increased oral levodopa produced large, sustained benefit, the basis of treatment ever since.

history.title: Thrombolysis for acute stroke
history.detail: The NINDS rt-PA trial showed that intravenous alteplase given within three hours of ischaemic stroke improved outcome. Later trials extended the time window and, in 2015, proved the benefit of thrombectomy for large vessel occlusion.
